name: Methohexital (Brevital Sodium)
summary: Ultra–short-acting IV anesthetic used to put you to sleep for ECT. Works immediately, wears off fast, and must be given with full airway and heart monitoring.
description: Methohexital is a fast on/off anesthetic that’s commonly used for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). The goal is simple: you’re asleep and not aware of the procedure, then you wake up quickly afterward. This medication can slow or stop breathing for short periods, drop blood pressure, and trigger airway spasm—so it’s only given in settings with continuous monitoring, resuscitation drugs, and staff trained in airway management.
patient_summary: For ECT, methohexital is the “lights out fast, wake up fast” anesthetic. It works immediately through the IV and usually wears off within minutes, but you still need close monitoring because breathing can slow or pause and blood pressure can dip. You should not drive or make important decisions the same day.

linked_conditions.context: Methohexital doesn’t treat depression or anxiety directly. It’s used to safely induce sleep for ECT so the procedure can be performed with comfort, immobility, and controlled airway/heart monitoring.

When ECT is used for severe catatonia, methohexital may be selected as the anesthetic because it has a rapid onset and short recovery profile, allowing repeated treatments while supporting close physiologic monitoring.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to methohexital or any component of the formulation
Any situation where general anesthesia is contraindicated

efficacy_response.metric: Time to clinical recovery after a single IV dose (ECT-style anesthesia)
efficacy_response.patient_text: For ECT anesthesia, “efficacy” isn’t about treating symptoms—it’s about reliable sleep induction and fast recovery so the procedure can be done safely. Most people wake up within minutes, but coordination and judgment can still be off for hours.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, methohexital is mainly used as the anesthetic for {link:condition:electroconvulsive-therapy:electroconvulsive therapy (ECT)}. It’s not a daily medication and it’s not “for anxiety” or “for depression” the way SSRIs are. It’s the short-acting sleep medicine that lets the ECT team do the treatment safely and humanely.
items: {link:condition:electroconvulsive-therapy:ECT anesthesia}: Rapid IV induction so you’re asleep during the procedure and can wake up soon after
Procedure support: Helps keep the body still and comfortable while the team monitors breathing, heart rhythm, and blood pressure

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: For ECT, most people don’t “feel” methohexital so much as they notice how fast everything happens. These are common experiences people describe:

quotes: I remember the IV… and then nothing.
It was basically instant—one second awake, next second I was out.
I didn’t feel myself falling asleep. It just happened.
I woke up pretty fast but felt groggy and confused for a bit.
I was awake in minutes, but my brain felt scrambled for a while.
I could talk, but I wouldn’t trust myself to make decisions.
items.note: Even if you wake up quickly, coordination and judgment can be off the rest of the day.

quotes: My throat felt scratchy like I’d been breathing through something.
I had mild nausea afterward, then it passed.
I felt shaky for a few minutes after waking up.
items.note: Some of this is the anesthesia itself, and some is the ECT procedure and recovery environment.

items.category: The Safety Vibe (It’s a Monitored Medication)
quotes: There were so many monitors—pulse ox, blood pressure, everything.
It felt intense, but also reassuring that they were watching everything.
It’s not a casual med. You can tell it’s serious.
items.note: This drug is designed to be used with continuous respiratory and cardiac monitoring, plus airway-ready staff and equipment.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Methohexital is built for speed: immediate sleep induction and fast recovery. That’s exactly why it’s often chosen for ECT.
key_points: Typical recovery window after a single dose: about 5–15 minutes to be awake and following commands
Psychomotor impairment can linger longer (hours), even if you feel “awake”

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.metric: Procedure success support (sleep induction + fast wake-up)
sections.text: For ECT, methohexital’s job is to reliably induce anesthesia quickly and wear off quickly. If the anesthesia is too light, people can move or become aware. If it’s too deep, breathing and blood pressure can become unsafe. The “win” is smooth induction, stable monitoring, and a controlled recovery—every single session.
sections.clinical_details: Clinicians titrate methohexital to the minimum effective anesthetic depth for the procedure while maintaining airway protection and cardiovascular stability. Because it can cause apnea, respiratory depression, hypotension, and laryngospasm, it’s used in settings equipped for continuous monitoring and immediate resuscitation.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: US BOXED WARNING: Only give in monitored medical settings with immediate airway rescue capability.
sections.black_box: Appropriate administration (US Boxed Warning): Methohexital should only be administered in hospitals or ambulatory care settings that provide continuous monitoring of respiratory and cardiac function. Resuscitative drugs and age- and size-appropriate equipment for bag/valve/mask ventilation and intubation must be immediately available, along with personnel trained in their use and skilled in airway management. For deeply sedated patients, a designated individual other than the practitioner performing the procedure should continuously monitor the patient.
other: Breathing risk: Can cause apnea and respiratory depression—airway and ventilation must be actively managed
Airway spasm: Laryngospasm can occur, especially during induction
Blood pressure/heart effects: May cause temporary hypotension and tachycardia; higher risk if medically unstable
IV safety: Extravasation or accidental intra-arterial injection can cause severe tissue injury/necrosis
Cumulative effect: Repeated dosing can stack and prolong sedation
patient_counseling: This is not an at-home medication. It’s given by a trained team with full monitoring.
Do not drive, drink alcohol, or make big decisions the day of treatment.
Tell the team if you have asthma/COPD, sleep apnea, heart disease, severe anemia, liver disease, kidney disease, or a seizure disorder.
Tell the team about every sedating medication or substance you use (benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep meds, alcohol, cannabis)—it can change safety and dosing.
If you develop severe shortness of breath, wheezing, chest pain, or fainting during recovery, that’s urgent—tell staff immediately.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most effects are short-lived and happen around the procedure: breathing suppression, airway irritation/spasm, blood pressure changes, nausea/vomiting, and injection-site pain. Because it’s an anesthetic, the side effects we care about most are airway and cardiovascular safety.
plain_language_list: Short pauses in breathing (apnea) or slowed breathing
Drop in blood pressure or fast heart rate
Pain or irritation at the injection site

common.patient_note: This can look like shallow breathing or brief pauses. In ECT settings, the team expects this possibility and monitors oxygenation continuously while supporting breathing as needed.
Blood pressure may dip temporarily and heart rate may rise. This matters most for people with heart disease or unstable blood pressure.
Some people experience coughing or hiccups. Rarely, the airway can spasm, which is why airway-skilled staff and equipment are required.
This can happen after anesthesia. The team can treat it in recovery if needed.
IV site discomfort can occur. Good IV access and proper dilution help reduce risk.

serious: Circulatory shock or severe circulatory depression (medical emergency)
Severe laryngospasm with impaired ventilation (medical emergency)
Anaphylaxis or severe hypersensitivity reaction (medical emergency)
Severe tissue injury/necrosis from extravasation or intra-arterial injection (medical emergency)
Seizure (reported postmarketing; in ECT settings seizure activity is procedure-related and medically managed, but unexpected events still require urgent assessment)

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: With methohexital, the big issue is additive brain-and-breathing suppression. Anything else that sedates you can make this medication more dangerous.

items.risk: Additive CNS and respiratory depression; worsened sedation and breathing risk.
items.action: Avoid alcohol before and after ECT sessions as instructed by your treatment team.

items.risk: Higher risk of respiratory depression, low oxygen, and oversedation.
items.action: Tell the anesthesia team about all opioid use. Dosing and monitoring plans may need adjustment.

items.with: Benzodiazepines, sleep meds, and other sedatives
items.risk: Stacked sedation and impaired breathing; can also affect ECT treatment planning.
items.action: Disclose all sedatives (including PRN). Your team may hold or adjust certain meds around ECT depending on safety and treatment goals.

items.with: Blood pressure medications and other agents that lower BP
items.risk: Greater risk of hypotension during induction.
items.action: Follow pre-ECT medication instructions. The team may adjust timing or dosing on treatment days.

items.risk: Significant interactions may require dose/frequency adjustment or avoidance.
items.action: Medication reconciliation matters. Bring an updated med list (including supplements) to every ECT session.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: For ECT, methohexital is given IV by the anesthesia team to induce general anesthesia quickly. Doses are weight-based and titrated to the minimum effective depth needed for the procedure, with continuous breathing and heart monitoring.

adult.ect_induction: IV: 1 to 1.5 mg/kg for induction; titrate to response and tolerability (typical ECT workflow: rapid IV bolus to sleep, then proceed with treatment under monitoring)
adult.ect_redose: If additional anesthetic is needed: IV redose 0.5 mg/kg based on response and tolerability (often in small increments per anesthesia judgment)

sections.simple_explanation: This medication works in seconds. The team gives enough to put you fully asleep for the procedure—no more than necessary—then supports breathing and blood pressure until you’re awake and stable in recovery.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Methohexital is a procedural anesthetic. Special population guidance is mostly about physiologic vulnerability (breathing, blood pressure, metabolism) and fetal/infant exposure rather than long-term psychiatric effects.
sections.pregnancy: Methohexital crosses the placenta. Repeated or prolonged exposure to anesthetic/sedative drugs during periods of rapid brain growth (including the third trimester) has been associated with neurodevelopmental concerns in animal data, and epidemiologic human studies report mixed signals. For medically necessary procedures, treatment should not be withheld solely due to pregnancy; for elective procedures, delaying may be considered when clinically appropriate. If anesthesia time is expected to be prolonged, the team should discuss benefits vs potential fetal risks.
sections.lactation: Methohexital is present in breast milk. Reported data suggest milk levels peak around ~1 hour after induction and become very low or not measurable later the same day; many protocols allow resuming breastfeeding once the parent is awake and stable in recovery for healthy, full-term infants. For infants at higher risk (apnea/hypotonia), extra caution and individualized guidance are appropriate.
sections.pediatrics: ECT in minors is uncommon and highly specialized. Pediatric anesthesia exposures raise specific neurodevelopmental warning language for repeated or lengthy sedation in very young children. If methohexital is used in pediatric patients for any procedure, dosing is weight-based and requires pediatric anesthesia expertise and full monitoring infrastructure.
sections.geriatrics: Older adults can be more sensitive to anesthetics and more prone to low blood pressure, airway events, prolonged grogginess, and falls after discharge. Use the low end of dosing ranges and titrate carefully. Plan for extra recovery time and strict same-day safety precautions (no driving, supervised discharge).
sections.hepatic: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment is provided, but methohexital is hepatically metabolized, so effects may be prolonged or stronger in hepatic impairment. Use caution and titrate carefully.
sections.renal: No formal manufacturer dose adjustment is provided; need for adjustment is generally unlikely because limited active drug is excreted in urine. Use caution in significant renal disease, especially when overall physiologic reserve is low.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Continuous respiratory monitoring: pulse oximetry; consider capnography when available
Airway readiness: immediate access to bag/valve/mask ventilation and intubation equipment; personnel skilled in airway management present
Continuous cardiovascular monitoring: heart rate/rhythm, blood pressure; watch for hypotension and tachycardia
Sedation depth and recovery: level of consciousness, protective reflexes, ability to maintain a patent airway, and safe ambulation before discharge
Signs of airway reactivity: cough, wheeze, bronchospasm, laryngospasm—especially in asthma/COPD
IV site monitoring: prevent extravasation; confirm appropriate IV access before administration
Post-procedure safety: psychomotor impairment can persist—confirm safe escort and no driving/operating machinery same day

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Methohexital for ECT is supplied as a reconstituted injectable product (vials), then diluted and administered IV by clinical staff.
items: Injection, reconstituted solution (as sodium): 500 mg vial (brand and generic available)
Typical working concentrations in practice: diluted to a maximum concentration of 1% (10 mg/mL) for IV use
IM solution (less relevant to ECT workflows): 5% (50 mg/mL) may be used in other contexts

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Methohexital is an ultra–short-acting barbiturate anesthetic. In plain terms: it turns down brain activity fast, producing deep sedation/anesthesia (sleep) within seconds. It depresses the sensory cortex, decreases motor activity, and alters cerebellar function—so you’re not aware, not moving, and not forming memories during the procedure.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Methohexital is not a psychiatric “treatment” in the way antidepressants, mood stabilizers, or therapy are. It’s the anesthetic that makes ECT possible. Think of it as the safety-critical backstage medication: rapid induction, short duration, tightly monitored, repeatable across multiple ECT sessions, and always administered by trained clinicians with airway and resuscitation capability.

seo.description: Methohexital (Brevital Sodium) is a fast on/off IV anesthetic commonly used for ECT. Learn how it works immediately, typical ECT induction dosing (1–1.5 mg/kg), key risks (apnea, hypotension, laryngospasm), required monitoring, and recovery precautions.

faqs.q: What is methohexital used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In psychiatry, methohexital is mainly used as the anesthetic for ECT. It doesn’t treat depression or anxiety directly—it’s the medication that puts you fully asleep so ECT can be done safely and comfortably.

faqs.q: How fast does methohexital work for ECT?
faqs.a: IV methohexital works immediately—usually within seconds. That fast onset is a big reason it’s commonly used for ECT anesthesia.

After a single IV dose, people often wake up within about 5–15 minutes. But “awake” doesn’t always mean fully back to baseline—coordination, reaction time, and judgment can still be impaired for hours.

faqs.q: Why does methohexital have a boxed warning?
faqs.a: Because it can suppress breathing and affect heart and blood pressure. It must be given only in hospitals or ambulatory settings with continuous respiratory and cardiac monitoring, immediate airway rescue equipment, and staff trained in airway management.

It can cause apnea (brief pauses in breathing) and respiratory depression. In ECT settings, this is why you’re continuously monitored and why the team is ready to support your airway and breathing immediately if needed.
No. It’s administered by clinicians as part of a procedure (like ECT) in a monitored medical setting. This is not a prescription you take at home.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects after methohexital during ECT?
faqs.a: Short-term grogginess, brief breathing suppression (managed by the team), blood pressure changes, nausea/vomiting, and sometimes coughing or throat irritation. Injection-site discomfort can also happen.

faqs.q: Can I drive after ECT if methohexital wears off quickly?
faqs.a: No. Even if you wake up fast, psychomotor impairment can linger. After ECT/anesthesia, you should not drive or operate machinery the same day and you should have a responsible adult escort you home.

faqs.q: Does methohexital interact with benzodiazepines or opioids?
faqs.a: Yes—sedatives can stack. Benzodiazepines, opioids, sleep meds, alcohol, and other CNS depressants can increase the risk of oversedation and breathing problems. Always disclose everything you take so the anesthesia team can plan safely.

faqs.q: Is methohexital safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It crosses the placenta, and anesthesia exposures in pregnancy require individualized risk-benefit discussion. It can also be present in breast milk; many protocols allow resuming breastfeeding once the parent is awake and stable in recovery for healthy, full-term infants, but higher-risk infants may require extra caution. Your team should guide you based on your situation.
